claim: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) is the main hub of the brain reward system.
source: The cellular architecture of the ventral tegmental area (VTA), the main hub of the brain reward system, remains only partially characterized.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the VTA.

claim: Three distinct subtypes of somatostatin (Sst)-expressing neurons exist in the mouse VTA.
source: To extend the characterization to inhibitory neurons, we have identified three distinct subtypes of somatostatin (Sst)-expressing neurons in the mouse VTA.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological clustering data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VTA Sst neuron subtypes differ in their electrophysiological properties.
source: These neurons differ in their electrophysiological and morphological properties, anatomical localization, as well as mRNA expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiological recordings and clustering analysis presented in Figures 2 and 3 and Table 1.

claim: VTA Sst neuron subtypes differ in their morphological properties.
source: These neurons differ in their electrophysiological and morphological properties, anatomical localization, as well as mRNA expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data presented in Figure 5.

claim: VTA Sst neuron subtypes differ in their anatomical localization.
source: These neurons differ in their electrophysiological and morphological properties, anatomical localization, as well as mRNA expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical distribution data presented in Figure 4.

claim: VTA Sst neuron subtypes differ in their mRNA expression profiles.
source: These neurons differ in their electrophysiological and morphological properties, anatomical localization, as well as mRNA expression profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by PatchSeq and in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Most VTA Sst neurons express GABAergic inhibitory markers.
source: Importantly, similar to cortical Sst-containing interneurons, most VTA Sst neurons express GABAergic inhibitory markers, but some of them also express glutamatergic excitatory markers and a subpopulation even express dopaminergic markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing 75% of Sst neurons are Slc32a1-positive (Figure 6b).

claim: Some VTA Sst neurons express glutamatergic excitatory markers.
source: Importantly, similar to cortical Sst-containing interneurons, most VTA Sst neurons express GABAergic inhibitory markers, but some of them also express glutamatergic excitatory markers and a subpopulation even express dopaminergic markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing 18% of Sst neurons are Slc17a6-positive (Figure 6b).

claim: A subpopulation of VTA Sst neurons express dopaminergic markers.
source: Importantly, similar to cortical Sst-containing interneurons, most VTA Sst neurons express GABAergic inhibitory markers, but some of them also express glutamatergic excitatory markers and a subpopulation even express dopaminergic markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing 1% of Sst neurons are Slc6a3-positive and PatchSeq data showing Delayed neurons express dopaminergic markers (Figure 6).

claim: Only some of the proposed marker genes for cortical Sst neurons are expressed in VTA Sst neurons.
source: Furthermore, only some of the proposed marker genes for cortical Sst neurons were expressed in the VTA Sst neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of gene expression between cortical and VTA Sst neurons presented in Figure 8.

claim: One of the VTA Sst neuron subtypes locally inhibits neighboring dopamine neurons.
source: Physiologically, one of the VTA Sst neuron subtypes locally inhibited neighboring dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic circuit mapping experiments showing ADP neurons evoke IPSCs in DA neurons (Figure 7).

claim: VTA Sst neurons are multifunctional players in the midbrain reward circuitry.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate the remarkable complexity and heterogeneity of VTA Sst neurons and suggest that these cells are multifunctional players in the midbrain reward circuitry.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the heterogeneity and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The VTA is the origin of dopaminergic projections in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways.
source: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the mammalian brain is the origin of dopaminergic projections in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways (Yamamoto and Vernier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamamoto and Vernier, 2011.

claim: Proper function of mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways is required for motivation and learning.
source: Proper function of these pathways is required for important behaviors such as motivation and learning (Schultz et al., 1997; Wise, 2005), with disturbances being associated with several pathological states including addiction among others (Korpi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schultz et al., 1997 and Wise, 2005.

claim: Disturbances in mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways are associated with addiction and other pathological states.
source: Proper function of these pathways is required for important behaviors such as motivation and learning (Schultz et al., 1997; Wise, 2005), with disturbances being associated with several pathological states including addiction among others (Korpi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Korpi et al., 2015.

claim: The VTA harbors a sizable population of neurons expressing γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
source: However, the VTA also harbors a sizable population of neurons expressing γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and a smaller population of glutamatergic (Glu) neurons (Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morales and Margolis, 2017.

claim: The VTA harbors a smaller population of glutamatergic neurons.
source: However, the VTA also harbors a sizable population of neurons expressing γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and a smaller population of glutamatergic (Glu) neurons (Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morales and Margolis, 2017.

claim: VTA GABA neurons regulate prediction error detection by VTA DA neurons.
source: Indeed, VTA GABA neurons are known to regulate prediction error detection by VTA DA neurons (Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eshel et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons strongly inhibits local DA neurons via GABAA receptors.
source: Further, optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons (identified by expression of glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 or the vesicular GABA transporter, Slc32a1) strongly inhibits local DA neurons via GABAA receptors, resulting in aversive place conditioning and reduced reward consumption (Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2012 and van Zessen et al., 2012.

claim: Optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons results in aversive place conditioning.
source: Further, optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons (identified by expression of glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 or the vesicular GABA transporter, Slc32a1) strongly inhibits local DA neurons via GABAA receptors, resulting in aversive place conditioning and reduced reward consumption (Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2012 and van Zessen et al., 2012.

claim: Optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons results in reduced reward consumption.
source: Further, optogenetic photostimulation of VTA GABA neurons (identified by expression of glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 or the vesicular GABA transporter, Slc32a1) strongly inhibits local DA neurons via GABAA receptors, resulting in aversive place conditioning and reduced reward consumption (Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2012 and van Zessen et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of VTA GABA projection neurons that inhibit cholinergic interneurons in the nucleus accumbens increases discrimination of aversive stimuli.
source: Activation of VTA GABA projection neurons that inhibit cholinergic interneurons in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) also increases discrimination of aversive stimuli (Brown et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of VTA GABA neurons is an important mechanism of action for opioids.
source: Finally, inhibition of VTA GABA neurons appears to be an important mechanism of action for pharmacological agents, such as opioids and GABAergic compounds (Johnson and North, 1992; Tan et al., 2010; Vashchinkina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and North, 1992; Tan et al., 2010; and Vashchinkina et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of VTA GABA neurons is an important mechanism of action for GABAergic compounds.
source: Finally, inhibition of VTA GABA neurons appears to be an important mechanism of action for pharmacological agents, such as opioids and GABAergic compounds (Johnson and North, 1992; Tan et al., 2010; Vashchinkina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and North, 1992; Tan et al., 2010; and Vashchinkina et al., 2014.

claim: There is ample evidence for great heterogeneity in interneuron subtypes in the cortex and other forebrain regions.
source: In the cortex and other forebrain regions, there is ample evidence for great heterogeneity in interneuron subtypes (Rudy et al., 2011; Pelkey et al., 2017; Krabbe et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rudy et al., 2011; Pelkey et al., 2017; Krabbe et al., 2018; and Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: The most common interneuron subtypes in the mouse cortex include somatostatin (Sst), parvalbumin (PV) and 5HT3A receptor-expressing neuronal populations.
source: In the mouse cortex, the most common interneuron subtypes include somatostatin (Sst), parvalbumin (PV) and 5HT3A receptor-expressing neuronal populations (Rudy et al., 2011), which can be manipulated using mouse Cre-lines (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rudy et al., 2011 and Taniguchi et al., 2011.

claim: GABA neuron subtypes in the basolateral amygdala differ from those of the cortex.
source: Indeed, even GABA neuron populations in the forebrain are not identical in all regions; for example, GABA neuron subtypes in the basolateral amygdala differ from those of the cortex (Krabbe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krabbe et al., 2018.

claim: Sst neurons in the VTA are fivefold more abundant than PV neurons.
source: Here, we focused on the Sst subtype of VTA neurons, which are fivefold more abundant than PV neurons and 50-fold more abundant than neurons expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Sst neurons in the VTA are 50-fold more abundant than neurons expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
source: Here, we focused on the Sst subtype of VTA neurons, which are fivefold more abundant than PV neurons and 50-fold more abundant than neurons expressing vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Sst neurons represent the most molecularly-diverse GABA neuronal population in the forebrain.
source: Moreover, in the forebrain, Sst neurons represent the most molecularly-diverse GABA neuronal population [more than 20 Sst-subtypes in the mouse visual cortex (Tasic et al., 2018)].
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: There are more than 20 Sst-subtypes in the mouse visual cortex.
source: Moreover, in the forebrain, Sst neurons represent the most molecularly-diverse GABA neuronal population [more than 20 Sst-subtypes in the mouse visual cortex (Tasic et al., 2018)].
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tasic et al., 2018.

claim: Sst neurons form two distinct clusters within the VTA area: lateral and medial.
source: Anatomically, Sst neurons formed two distinct clusters within the VTA area: lateral and medial.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data presented in Figure 1a.

claim: The lateral cluster of Sst neurons is located in the parabrachial pigmented (PBP) nucleus.
source: The lateral cluster was located in the largest VTA nucleus, the parabrachial pigmented (PBP) nucleus, while the medial cluster was in the more caudal part of the VTA, within the parainterfascicular (PIF) and paranigral nuclei (PN) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data presented in Figure 1a.

claim: The medial cluster of Sst neurons is located in the parainterfascicular (PIF) and paranigral nuclei (PN).
source: The lateral cluster was located in the largest VTA nucleus, the parabrachial pigmented (PBP) nucleus, while the medial cluster was in the more caudal part of the VTA, within the parainterfascicular (PIF) and paranigral nuclei (PN) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data presented in Figure 1a.

claim: The number of VTA Sst cells is approximately 12% of the number of Th-positive neurons using immunohistochemical counting.
source: Initial cell counting using tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) immunohistochemical staining and Sst-Cre-linked cell marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) yielded an estimate for the number of VTA Sst cells of approximately 12% of the number of Th-positive neurons (809 ± 205 cells vs. 6800 ± 1080 cells, n = 3, here and after mean ± SEM, from bregma −2.8 to −3.8 mm).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical cell counting data.

claim: About 10% of Sst-positive cells co-stain with a Th antibody.
source: About 10% of the Sst-positive cells co-stained with a Th antibody.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical co-staining data.

claim: The density of Sst cells increases in the rostrocaudal direction, starting from bregma −3.5.
source: The density of Sst cells increased in the rostrocaudal direction, starting from bregma −3.5, which was the opposite to that of Th+ neurons, which decreased in number starting from the same level (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data presented in Figure 1b-c.

claim: The density of Th+ neurons decreases in the rostrocaudal direction, starting from bregma −3.5.
source: The density of Sst cells increased in the rostrocaudal direction, starting from bregma −3.5, which was the opposite to that of Th+ neurons, which decreased in number starting from the same level (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data presented in Figure 1b-c.

claim: The total number of VTA Sst neurons is approximately 1500 in adult mice using in situ hybridization.
source: Estimates of the total number of cells were higher using this method (Sst: 1120 ± 470 cells vs. Slc6a3: 14600 ± 1610 cells, n = 4, from bregma −3.07 to −3.88 mm) and is in line with recent estimates of 1500 Sst neurons in the VTA of adult mice (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data and is consistent with a citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: ADP neurons demonstrate a prominent afterdepolarization of 13.8 ± 0.5 mV after an action potential.
source: The names we have assigned these neurons are based on their distinctive features: afterdepolarizing (ADP) neurons demonstrated a prominent afterdepolarization (13.8 ± 0.5 mV, n = 215) after an action potential (AP; Figure 2a);
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings presented in Figure 2a and Table 1.

claim: HFF neurons have the highest maximal rate of AP firing at 129 ± 5 Hz.
source: high-frequency firing (HFF) neurons had the highest maximal rate of AP firing (129 ± 5 Hz, n = 92; Figure 2b);
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings presented in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Delayed neurons fire APs with a significant time delay of 279 ± 20 ms after the start of a depolarizing current.
source: while delayed neurons fired APs with a significant time delay (279 ± 20 ms, n = 85) after the start of a depolarizing current, even at the high levels of depolarization (Figure 2c) (Video 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings presented in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: The presence of three neuron subtypes was confirmed by combining principal component analysis (PCA) with unsupervised clustering via a Gaussian mixture model (GMM).
source: The presence of three neuron subtypes was confirmed by combining principal component analysis (PCA) of 25 electrophysiological features with unsupervised clustering via a Gaussian mixture model (GMM).
evidence: This is based on the clustering analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: HFF neurons have the lowest current thresholds among the three Sst neuron subtypes.
source: Thus, HFF neurons had the lowest current thresholds and produced the largest number of APs at both the lowest and highest levels of excitation (3.9 ± 0.2, F(2, 389)=80.71; p<0.0001, and 39.1 ± 3.1, F(2, 389)=58.70; p<0.0001, during 800 ms depolarization) as compared to other two subtypes.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: HFF neurons produce the largest number of APs at both the lowest and highest levels of excitation compared to other two subtypes.
source: Thus, HFF neurons had the lowest current thresholds and produced the largest number of APs at both the lowest and highest levels of excitation (3.9 ± 0.2, F(2, 389)=80.71; p<0.0001, and 39.1 ± 3.1, F(2, 389)=58.70; p<0.0001, during 800 ms depolarization) as compared to other two subtypes.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Brief, prominent afterhyperpolarizations and the narrowest APs are distinctive features of HFF neurons.
source: Brief, prominent afterhyperpolarizations (AHPs) and the narrowest APs were also distinctive features of this neuron subtype, consistent with the ability of these cells to fire APs at high frequency.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Delayed neurons show low excitability with the highest threshold current of 40.8 ± 4.3 pA.
source: Delayed neurons showed low excitability, with the highest threshold current (40.8 ± 4.3 pA, F (2, 389)=46.83; p<0.0001), broadest and slowest decaying APs.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Delayed neurons have the broadest and slowest decaying APs among the three Sst neuron subtypes.
source: Delayed neurons showed low excitability, with the highest threshold current (40.8 ± 4.3 pA, F (2, 389)=46.83; p<0.0001), broadest and slowest decaying APs.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: ADP neurons tend to have lower input resistance of 783 ± 24 MΩ compared to other subtypes.
source: In addition to their prominent ADPs, ADP neurons tended to have lower input resistance (783 ± 24 MΩ, F(2, 389)=5.121; p=0.0064) and higher level of AP frequency adaptation (0.28 ± 0.02);
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: ADP neurons have a higher level of AP frequency adaptation of 0.28 ± 0.02.
source: In addition to their prominent ADPs, ADP neurons tended to have lower input resistance (783 ± 24 MΩ, F(2, 389)=5.121; p=0.0064) and higher level of AP frequency adaptation (0.28 ± 0.02);
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: ADP neurons are the most abundant Sst neuron subtype.
source: otherwise, these neurons were intermediate in their electrical properties and were the most abundant Sst neuron subtype.
evidence: This is based on the sample sizes reported in the electrophysiological experiments (n=215 ADP, n=92 HFF, n=85 Delayed).

claim: The three electrophysiological subtypes remain the same in young (P20) and adult (P90) animals.
source: To examine whether these three electrophysiological subtypes are restricted to only early developmental stages, we also recorded from an additional 92 Sst neurons from adult (P90) animals and added them to the dataset of juvenile mice. Re-clustering of the data defined the same three clusters and the 92 additional neurons (black circled dots in Figure 3a) mingled with juvenile cells, indicating that the subtypes remained the same in young (P20) and adult (P90) animals.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from adult mice and re-clustering analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Most ADP neurons (64%) are found in the lateral VTA, predominantly in the PBP nucleus.
source: Most ADP (64%) and HFF (71%) neurons were found in the lateral VTA, predominantly in the PBP nucleus (Figure 4a–b),
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Most HFF neurons (71%) are found in the lateral VTA, predominantly in the PBP nucleus.
source: Most ADP (64%) and HFF (71%) neurons were found in the lateral VTA, predominantly in the PBP nucleus (Figure 4a–b),
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Most Delayed neurons (79%) are located in the medial part of the VTA.
source: whereas Delayed neurons were primarily in the medial part of the VTA (79%) and almost equally distributed between the PIF and PN nuclei.
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Delayed neurons are almost equally distributed between the PIF and PN nuclei.
source: whereas Delayed neurons were primarily in the medial part of the VTA (79%) and almost equally distributed between the PIF and PN nuclei.
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A larger proportion of ADP neurons (71%) reside within the ventral VTA.
source: From a ventrodorsal view, a larger proportion of ADP (71%) and HFF (59%) neurons resided within the ventral VTA, while most Delayed neurons (84%) were located in its dorsal part.
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A larger proportion of HFF neurons (59%) reside within the ventral VTA.
source: From a ventrodorsal view, a larger proportion of ADP (71%) and HFF (59%) neurons resided within the ventral VTA, while most Delayed neurons (84%) were located in its dorsal part.
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Most Delayed neurons (84%) are located in the dorsal part of the VTA.
source: From a ventrodorsal view, a larger proportion of ADP (71%) and HFF (59%) neurons resided within the ventral VTA, while most Delayed neurons (84%) were located in its dorsal part.
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: VTA Sst neurons have a relatively simple structure with thin and faintly branching processes that extend up to 1 cm from the cell body.
source: The cells had a relatively simple structure, with thin and faintly branching processes that extended up to 1 cm from the cell body (Figure 5a–c; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on morphological reconstruction data presented in Figure 5.

claim: VTA Sst cell body areas range from 120 to 190 µm2.
source: Cell body areas ranged from 120 to 190 µm2 (measured in 2D); this is substantially smaller than the cell body area of dopaminergic neurons, which was measured as 294 ± 4 µm2 (n = 10) in our optical mapping experiments (see below).
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements presented in Figure 5.

claim: VTA Sst cell body area is substantially smaller than the cell body area of dopaminergic neurons (294 ± 4 µm2).
source: Cell body areas ranged from 120 to 190 µm2 (measured in 2D); this is substantially smaller than the cell body area of dopaminergic neurons, which was measured as 294 ± 4 µm2 (n = 10) in our optical mapping experiments (see below).
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements.

claim: VTA Sst cells have 6–9 processes with 2–4 branching points.
source: VTA Sst cells had 6–9 processes with 2–4 branching points (Figure 5a; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on morphological reconstruction data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The structure of Delayed neurons is significantly different from those of ADP and HFF neurons.
source: The structure of Delayed neurons was significantly different from those of the other Sst neurons, as indicated by Sholl plots of neuronal process complexity (Figure 5c; n = 20).
evidence: This is based on Sholl analysis presented in Figure 5c.

claim: Delayed neurons differ from ADP and HFF neurons in their number of processes, branching points and cell body area.
source: Indeed, Delayed neurons were different from ADP and HFF neurons in their number of processes, branching points and cell body area (Figure 5a);
evidence: This is based on morphological measurements presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Four out of eight tested Delayed neurons were Th-positive.
source: Staining of filled neurons with anti-Th antibody revealed another unique feature of the Delayed neurons: four out of eight tested cells were Th-positive (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which was not observed in the two other Sst neuron subtypes.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Th-positivity was not observed in ADP and HFF Sst neuron subtypes.
source: Staining of filled neurons with anti-Th antibody revealed another unique feature of the Delayed neurons: four out of eight tested cells were Th-positive (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which was not observed in the two other Sst neuron subtypes.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining data.

claim: 75% of Sst neurons are Slc32a1-positive (GABAergic).
source: We observed four main expression patterns for Sst neurons: 75% were Slc32a1-positive, 18% Slc17a6-positive, 5% Slc32a1+Slc17a6 positive, 1% Slc6a3-positive and the remaining 1% included all other possible combinations (Slc17a6+ Slc6a3, Slc32a1+ Slc6a3 and Slc17a6+Slc32a1+ Slc6a3) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on multichannel in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6a-b.

claim: 18% of Sst neurons are Slc17a6-positive (glutamatergic).
source: We observed four main expression patterns for Sst neurons: 75% were Slc32a1-positive, 18% Slc17a6-positive, 5% Slc32a1+Slc17a6 positive, 1% Slc6a3-positive and the remaining 1% included all other possible combinations (Slc17a6+ Slc6a3, Slc32a1+ Slc6a3 and Slc17a6+Slc32a1+ Slc6a3) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on multichannel in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6a-b.

claim: 5% of Sst neurons are Slc32a1+Slc17a6 positive (both GABAergic and glutamatergic).
source: We observed four main expression patterns for Sst neurons: 75% were Slc32a1-positive, 18% Slc17a6-positive, 5% Slc32a1+Slc17a6 positive, 1% Slc6a3-positive and the remaining 1% included all other possible combinations (Slc17a6+ Slc6a3, Slc32a1+ Slc6a3 and Slc17a6+Slc32a1+ Slc6a3) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on multichannel in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6a-b.

claim: 1% of Sst neurons are Slc6a3-positive (dopaminergic).
source: We observed four main expression patterns for Sst neurons: 75% were Slc32a1-positive, 18% Slc17a6-positive, 5% Slc32a1+Slc17a6 positive, 1% Slc6a3-positive and the remaining 1% included all other possible combinations (Slc17a6+ Slc6a3, Slc32a1+ Slc6a3 and Slc17a6+Slc32a1+ Slc6a3) (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: This is based on multichannel in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Of 69 Sst neurons sequenced, 61 passed quality control criteria at all steps of analysis.
source: Of the 69 Sst neurons sequenced, 61/69 passed our quality control criteria at all steps of analysis.
evidence: This is based on the PatchSeq experimental data.

claim: All except one PatchSeq cell showed Sst gene expression.
source: All except one evinced Sst gene expression.
evidence: This is based on the PatchSeq experimental data.

claim: Five out of nine HFF cells were exclusively in the GABAergic cluster.
source: Five out of nine HFF cells were exclusively in the GABAergic cluster (main marker genes were Gad2, Gad1, Slc32a1, Atp1b1, Snap25, Camta1, Nrxn3, Gata3, Ttc3, Atp1a3, Nsf, Syn2, Sncb and Kcnc1) and two out of nine went also to a glutamatergic cluster (main markers were Slc17a6, Cacna2d1, Cbln2, Scn2a1, Shox2 and Adcyap1), thus being both GABAergic and glutamatergic.
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Two out of nine HFF cells mapped to both GABAergic and glutamatergic clusters.
source: Five out of nine HFF cells were exclusively in the GABAergic cluster (main marker genes were Gad2, Gad1, Slc32a1, Atp1b1, Snap25, Camta1, Nrxn3, Gata3, Ttc3, Atp1a3, Nsf, Syn2, Sncb and Kcnc1) and two out of nine went also to a glutamatergic cluster (main markers were Slc17a6, Cacna2d1, Cbln2, Scn2a1, Shox2 and Adcyap1), thus being both GABAergic and glutamatergic.
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Eight out of 43 ADP neurons were assigned exclusively to the GABAergic cluster.
source: Eight out of 43 ADP neurons were assigned exclusively to the GABAergic cluster, whereas most of these cells (26/43) went to both GABAergic and glutamatergic clusters.
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Most ADP neurons (26/43) mapped to both GABAergic and glutamatergic clusters.
source: Eight out of 43 ADP neurons were assigned exclusively to the GABAergic cluster, whereas most of these cells (26/43) went to both GABAergic and glutamatergic clusters.
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Eight out of nine Delayed neurons mapped onto a dopaminergic cell type.
source: Eight out of nine Delayed neurons mapped onto a dopaminergic cell type (main markers were: Slc6a3, Slc18a2, Th, Dlk1, Ret, Ddc, Aldh1a1, Cplx1, Cpne7, Pbx1, Syt1, Rab3c, Slc10a4, Cplx2, Erc2, Chrna4, En1, Epha5 and Chrna6).
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Only Delayed cells were assigned to the DA cluster.
source: Although six out of nine Delayed cells went also to the glutamatergic cluster, only Delayed cells were assigned to the DA cluster.
evidence: This is based on mapping PatchSeq data to reference scRNA-seq clusters.

claim: Delayed neurons express higher levels of DA markers (Th, Slc6a3, Ddc, Slc18a2) compared to ADP and HFF neurons.
source: Because the Delayed cluster included all variants of dopaminergic molecular subtypes, we examined DA marker expression in the PatchSeq data. Delayed neurons expressed higher levels of DA markers, such as Th, Slc6a3 (dopamine transporter), Ddc and Slc18a2 (VMAT2), compared to two other neuron subtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on PatchSeq gene expression data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Photostimulation of ADP neurons evokes inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in neighboring VTA DA neurons.
source: Photostimulation of ChR2-expressing ADP neurons (Figure 7a) evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in neighboring VTA DA neurons (Figure 7b–d).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic circuit mapping experiments presented in Figure 7.

claim: Evoked IPSCs were observed in 42% of DA cells examined (11/26 confirmed DA neurons).
source: We observed evoked IPSCs in 42% of DA cells examined (11/26 confirmed DA neurons).
evidence: This is based on optogenetic circuit mapping experiments.

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs were completely blocked by the GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine (10 µM).
source: Optically evoked IPSCs were completely blocked by the GABAA receptor antagonist, gabazine (10 µM, n = 2), indicating that Sst ADP neurons inhibit DA cells via GABAA receptors (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments presented in Figure 7b.

claim: Sst ADP neurons inhibit DA cells via GABAA receptors.

claim: The median size of input fields from ADP neurons to DA cells is 7400 μm2.
source: Further evidence for this comes from quantification of input field size: the median size of these input fields (7400 μm2; n = 11) was much larger than that of the optical footprint of individual ADP cells (640 μm2; n = 20), indicating that more than one presynaptic Sst ADP neuron must contribute to an inhibitory input field.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic circuit mapping measurements.

claim: The median size of the optical footprint of individual ADP cells is 640 μm2.
source: Further evidence for this comes from quantification of input field size: the median size of these input fields (7400 μm2; n = 11) was much larger than that of the optical footprint of individual ADP cells (640 μm2; n = 20), indicating that more than one presynaptic Sst ADP neuron must contribute to an inhibitory input field.
evidence: This is based on optogenetic circuit mapping measurements.

claim: More than one presynaptic Sst ADP neuron contributes to an inhibitory input field on DA cells.

evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of input field size to optical footprint size.

claim: DA neurons in the VTA are inhibited by multiple ADP neurons.
source: In conclusion, our optogenetic mapping experiments indicate that DA neurons in the VTA are inhibited by multiple ADP neurons, establishing ADP cells as inhibitory interneurons that converge upon postsynaptic DA cells.
evidence: This is based on the optogenetic circuit mapping experiments presented in Figure 7.

claim: ADP cells are inhibitory interneurons that converge upon postsynaptic DA cells.
source: In conclusion, our optogenetic mapping experiments indicate that DA neurons in the VTA are inhibited by multiple ADP neurons, establishing ADP cells as inhibitory interneurons that converge upon postsynaptic DA cells.
evidence: This is based on the optogenetic circuit mapping experiments presented in Figure 7.

claim: Lateral DA neurons project predominantly to the lateral shell of the NAc and respond to reward-related events.
source: Distinct anatomical locations of Sst cells within the VTA may indicate different physiological functions: lateral and medial Sst neuron clusters co-localize with previously described DA neuron populations (Lammel et al., 2011). Lateral DA neurons project predominantly to the lateral shell of the NAc and respond to reward-related events;
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lammel et al., 2011.

claim: Medial-posterior DA neurons project to the medial prefrontal cortex and medial shell of the NAc and undergo plastic changes after aversive stimuli.
source: in contrast, medial-posterior DA neurons project to the medial prefrontal cortex and medial shell of the NAc and undergo plastic changes after aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lammel et al., 2011 (referenced in the previous sentence).

claim: Sst ADP neurons may control the activity of DA neurons in the lateral VTA, thereby modulating reward processing and motivation signals.
source: It is possible that Sst ADP neurons, which are predominantly located in the lateral VTA and inhibit neighboring DA neurons, can control the activity of DA neurons in that particular area, thereby modulating reward processing and motivation signals, as previously established for the lateral VTA GABA neurons (Eshel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the anatomical location and functional properties of ADP neurons, with reference to Eshel et al., 2015.

claim: ADP cells may be targets for rewarding drugs such as opioids, gamma-hydroxybutyrate, benzodiazepines and other GABAergic drugs.
source: As local interneurons, ADP cells may also be targets for rewarding drugs, such as opioids (Johnson and North, 1992), gamma-hydroxybutyrate (Cruz et al., 2004) and benzodiazepines and other GABAergic drugs (Tan et al., 2010; Vashchinkina et al., 2014), which act via a disinhibitory mechanism by inhibiting local VTA GABA neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the properties of ADP neurons and supported by citations to Johnson and North, 1992; Cruz et al., 2004; Tan et al., 2010; and Vashchinkina et al., 2014.

claim: Sst ADP neurons play an important role in VTA physiology and pharmacological responses.
source: Thus, our results strongly suggest that Sst ADP neurons play an important role in VTA physiology and pharmacological responses.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the functional data and anatomical location of ADP neurons.

claim: VTA Sst neurons have lower cell capacitance than DA neurons.
source: VTA Sst neurons had a lower cell capacitance than DA neurons, reflecting the smaller cell size of Sst neurons compared to DA neurons. The mean capacitance of the three subtypes of Sst cells was 14 pF (Table 1), compared to the mean of 41 pF for DA neurons (taken from several studies summarized in https://neuroelectro.org/neuron/203/).
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological data from this study with published data on DA neurons.

claim: VTA Sst neurons have higher input resistance (849 vs. 665 MΩ) than DA neurons.
source: Higher input resistance (849 vs. 665 MΩ) and larger AP amplitude (92 vs. 66 mV), as well as narrower action potential half-width (1.1 vs. 2.8 ms) and more hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (−67.5 vs. −51.7 mV) were additional distinctive features of Sst neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological data from this study with published data on DA neurons.

claim: Delayed neurons resemble DA neurons in many respects.
source: Delayed neurons differed strongly from two other subtypes and, in many respects, resemble DA neurons. Indeed, they showed a wide action potential half-width, relatively large cell bodies and more highly branched dendrites as well as Th+ immunoreactivity, which are all common features of DA cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of morphological and electrophysiological properties of Delayed neurons with known properties of DA neurons.

claim: Delayed Sst neurons may represent a population of Sst-expressing DA neurons in the VTA.
source: Therefore, Delayed Sst neurons may represent a population of Sst-expressing DA neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the properties of Delayed neurons.

claim: About two thirds of marker genes identified for neocortical Sst neurons were expressed in the midbrain dataset or in the PatchSeq samples.
source: About two thirds of marker genes identified in Tasic et al., 2018 for neocortical Sst neurons were expressed in the midbrain dataset or in the PatchSeq samples (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Tac2 shows high expression in the neocortical dataset but is absent or lowly expressed in the midbrain and PatchSeq datasets.
source: Tac2, a marker gene of two different subtypes of neocortical Sst neurons (Tac2-Myh4 and Tac2-Tacstd2), as well as some cortical interneuron markers Crh, Npy and Pdyn genes (Sugino et al., 2006), showed a high expression in the neocortical dataset, but were absent or lowly expressed in the midbrain and PatchSeq datasets.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Cortical interneuron markers Crh, Npy and Pdyn show high expression in the neocortical dataset but are absent or lowly expressed in the midbrain and PatchSeq datasets.
source: Tac2, a marker gene of two different subtypes of neocortical Sst neurons (Tac2-Myh4 and Tac2-Tacstd2), as well as some cortical interneuron markers Crh, Npy and Pdyn genes (Sugino et al., 2006), showed a high expression in the neocortical dataset, but were absent or lowly expressed in the midbrain and PatchSeq datasets.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8 and supported by a citation to Sugino et al., 2006.

claim: Chodl, Nr2f2 and Necab1 show very low levels of expression in the PatchSeq and midbrain datasets.
source: Interestingly, Chodl, a gene expressed in the long-range Sst projection neurons of the neocortex (Tasic et al., 2016), and Nr2f2 and Necab1 showed very low levels of expression in the PatchSeq and midbrain datasets, while Calb2 and Nos1 were more pronounced in the PatchSeq cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8 and supported by a citation to Tasic et al., 2016.

claim: Calb2 and Nos1 are more pronounced in the PatchSeq cells compared to other datasets.
source: Interestingly, Chodl, a gene expressed in the long-range Sst projection neurons of the neocortex (Tasic et al., 2016), and Nr2f2 and Necab1 showed very low levels of expression in the PatchSeq and midbrain datasets, while Calb2 and Nos1 were more pronounced in the PatchSeq cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Sst neurons in VTA and midbrain have higher expression of glutamatergic (Slc17a6) and dopaminergic markers (Th, Slc6a3, Ddc) than those in the neocortex.
source: On the other hand, Sst neurons in VTA and midbrain Sst neurons had higher expression of glutamatergic (Slc17a6) and dopaminergic markers (Th, Slc6a3, Ddc) than those in the neocortex, suggesting a low level of combinatorial neurotransmitter phenotypes in the cortex as compared to the midbrain within the Sst neurons.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data presented in Figure 8.

claim: There is a low level of combinatorial neurotransmitter phenotypes in cortical Sst neurons compared to midbrain Sst neurons.
source: On the other hand, Sst neurons in VTA and midbrain Sst neurons had higher expression of glutamatergic (Slc17a6) and dopaminergic markers (Th, Slc6a3, Ddc) than those in the neocortex, suggesting a low level of combinatorial neurotransmitter phenotypes in the cortex as compared to the midbrain within the Sst neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of gene expression patterns.

claim: Nrxn3 shows robust expression in PatchSeq and midbrain Sst neurons.
source: Most of the developmental marker genes (Chen et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017) were poorly expressed in PatchSeq and midbrain Sst neurons, but interestingly, Nrxn3, a gene for neurexin 3, a presynaptic terminal protein stabilizing glutamate synapses (Dai et al., 2019) and serving as a candidate susceptibility gene for neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism (Wang et al., 2018), showed robust expression in PatchSeq and midbrain Sst neurons (Figure 8), in line with the expression of glutamatergic markers.
evidence: This is based on gene expression data presented in Figure 8 and supported by citations to Chen et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2019; and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: The VTA and midbrain Sst neurons clearly differ from the more heterogeneous neocortical Sst neurons.
source: These comparisons suggest that the VTA and midbrain Sst neurons clearly differ from the more heterogeneous neocortical Sst neurons, indicating a smaller number of molecular subtypes of neurons in the midbrain than cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the gene expression comparisons presented in Figure 8.

claim: There is a smaller number of molecular subtypes of Sst neurons in the midbrain than in the cortex.
